newsitem.title: GERMANY: Refugees not cheating way to Germany-Jewish leader.
newsitem.headline: Refugees not cheating way to Germany-Jewish leader.

text.p: The leader of Germany's Jewish community dismissed media reports that refugees from the former Soviet Union were gaining entry to Germany by claiming to be Jewish when they were not, a magazine reported on Friday.
Ignatz Bubis said some non-Jews had come to Germany under a decision in 1990 to accept an unlimited number of former Soviet Jews on humanitarian grounds.
But he said these people had accompanied Jewish relatives and were also entitled to immigrate to Germany.

"Some of these people are not Jewish. But they have Jewish family members and are allowed to travel with them. Of some 55,000 immigrants (to Germany) in the last seven years, about 30,000 are Jewish," Bubis told Focus magazine.
The German Foreign Ministry said in a statement there had been some abuse of the 1990 decision and said they were fighting this fraudulent practice.
The ministry denied reports Bonn wanted to restrict the influx of refugees because many were no longer persecuted or sought to emigrate out of purely economic reasons.
"Jewish immigrants from the former Soviet Union are welcome in Germany," ministry spokesman Martin Erdmann said.
Germany's Jews hoped the decision to allow Jews from the former Soviet Union to live in Germany would help to revive a community virtually wiped out by the Nazi Holocaust.

But Bubis told Focus magazine in an interview released ahead of publication on Saturday that some German consulates in former Soviet republics had used the crackdown on fraudulent entry as an excuse to stop Jews moving to Germany.
Bubis accused some consulate officials of anti-Semitism, saying they had blocked applications by claiming the refugees were not really Jewish.
"It's not the refugees who are committing fraud -- it's the diplomats. They should just admit they don't want to let any (Jews) in," said Bubis.
The ministry admitted some applications should not have been turned down, but said the errors had been corrected.
"It is difficult to check individual cases because old and damaged documents must be examined. Consular staff often work under tough conditions. But they do their best," Erdmann said.
